avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, bilateral facial diplegia variant

differential.key_features: Endemic exposure, erythema migrans, CSF Lyme serology cover.
Chest imaging, CSF ACE, MRI; cranial nerve VII commonly involved.
Diagnosis of exclusion; CSF dissociation and limb areflexia redirect to GBS.
Preserved reflexes; CSF normal; AChR antibodies / RNS distinguish.

key_clinical_evidence: Bilateral simultaneous facial diplegia is rarely idiopathic; GBS, Lyme, and sarcoidosis dominate the differential.
Limb areflexia and CSF dissociation tip the diagnosis toward GBS.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

patient.chief_complaint: One-day sudden-onset bilateral facial paralysis with loss of taste, drooling, and inability to close eyes — no limb weakness.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. H. is a 36-year-old IT specialist presenting with a 1-day history of sudden-onset bilateral facial paralysis. He awoke this morning unable to close either eye completely, with bilateral drooping of both cheeks, inability to purse his lips, and drooling of saliva. He cannot close his eyes, frown, show his teeth, blow, or whistle. He has lost taste bilaterally and has mild slurring of speech. There is no earache, hearing change, tinnitus, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, or fever. He has no limb weakness or sensory symptoms. There is no history of recent infection, travel, sick contacts, insect bites, or trauma. He does not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. He has never had a similar episode. His primary care physician initially considered Bell's palsy but was concerned because bilateral simultaneous facial palsy is rare and strongly suggests an underlying systemic process. The finding of globally diminished reflexes on neurological exam, despite the patient's primary complaint being facial, raises the clinical suspicion for a broader peripheral neuropathy.

neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 3.2 L (predicted 4.4 L — 73%). NIF: -42 cmH2O. No preceding illness, no recent travel, no sick contacts, no insect bites. Bilateral simultaneous facial nerve palsy — bilateral Bell's palsy is rare and should trigger systemic workup.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral complete facial paralysis — unable to close either eye, bilateral lagophthalmos with Bell's phenomenon preserved. Unable to clench teeth, frown, show teeth, blow, or whistle. Nasolabial folds absent bilaterally. Drooling. Loss of taste bilaterally. Slurred speech. No ptosis. Pupils equal and reactive. Full extraocular movements. No diplopia.
neurological_exam.gait: Slightly unsteady — can walk with careful monitoring.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral lower extremity: hip flexion 4/5, knee extension 4+/5 bilaterally. Upper extremity 4+/5.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Diminished deep tendon reflexes throughout — ankle jerks absent bilaterally, patellar and upper extremity 1+.
